dss_manuscripts.dss_text: מ עמל נפשו יראה אור ישבע ב דעתו יצדיק צדיק עבדי ל רבים ו עונתם הוא יסבול

divergences.mt_reading: יִרְאֶה יִשְׂבָּע (He will see, he will be satisfied)
divergences.lxx_reading: δεῖξαι αὐτῷ φῶς (to show him light)
divergences.dss_reading: יראה אור ישבע (He will see light, he will be satisfied)
divergences.textual_implication: The addition of אור ('light') in 1QIsa-a creates a direct object for the verb 'see' and aligns with the LXX reading φῶς, suggesting the LXX translator had a Hebrew Vorlage containing this word, which was later omitted in the proto-MT tradition through haplography or deliberate scribal shortening.
The 1QIsa-a reading agrees with MT in substance, using the same root דעת, though with typical Qumran orthographic variations including fuller spelling conventions common to the scroll.

divergences.mt_reading: יַצְדִּיק צַדִּיק (will justify, a righteous one)
divergences.lxx_reading: δικαιῶσαι δίκαιον (to justify a righteous one)
divergences.dss_reading: יצדיק צדיק (will justify, a righteous one)
divergences.textual_implication: 1QIsa-a preserves the same consonantal text as MT, supporting the antiquity of this difficult construction where the servant 'justifies' (makes righteous) despite the syntactic awkwardness.

dss_manuscripts.overall_note: 1QIsa-a provides crucial evidence for a major textual variant with the addition of אור, demonstrating that the LXX's reference to 'light' reflects an authentic Hebrew reading, not a translator's interpretive expansion. This scroll thus witnesses to a Hebrew text-form closer to the LXX Vorlage than to proto-MT. The variant has significant theological implications for understanding the Servant's vindication and aligns with light imagery elsewhere in Isaiah 40-66.

pesh_witness.pesh_text: ܘܡܢ ܥܡܠܐ ܕܢܦܫܗ ܢܚܙܐ ܘܢܣܒܥ ܒܝܕܥܬܐ ܘܢܙܟܐ ܠܙܕܝ̈ܩܐ ܥܒܕܐ ܗܘ ܕܣ̈ܓܝܐܐ ܘܚ̈ܛܗܝܗܘܢ ܗܘ ܢܣܒܘܠ

divergences.mt_reading: יִרְאֶה יִשְׂבָּע (He will see, he will be satisfied)
divergences.lxx_reading: δεῖξαι αὐτῷ φῶς (to show him light)
divergences.pesh_reading: ܢܚܙܐ ܘܢܣܒܥ (nḥze w-nesba' - he will see and be satisfied)
divergences.textual_implication: The Peshitta lacks an explicit object for 'see', suggesting either a Vorlage without אור or that the translator found the object implicit. The simple coordination with waw differs from both MT's asyndetic construction and LXX's infinitival structure, possibly reflecting inner-Syriac smoothing of a difficult Hebrew construction.

Peshitta uses the emphatic state without pronominal suffix, creating ambiguity whether 'knowledge' refers to the Servant's knowledge or knowledge about him. This may reflect translation technique that generalizes specific pronominal references, or a different parsing of the Hebrew syntax.

divergences.mt_reading: יַצְדִּיק צַדִּיק (will justify, a righteous one)
divergences.lxx_reading: δικαιῶσαι δίκαιον (to justify a righteous one)
divergences.pesh_reading: ܘܢܙܟܐ ܠܙܕܝ̈ܩܐ (w-nzake l-zaddiqē - and he will justify the righteous ones)
divergences.textual_implication: The Peshitta reads צדיק as plural 'righteous ones' rather than singular, possibly interpreting the construct as referring to the many who are made righteous. This reading harmonizes with 'many' (רבים) later in the verse and may represent theological interpretation emphasizing corporate salvation rather than ambiguous singular reference.

divergences.pesh_reading: ܥܒܕܐ ܗܘ (ʿabdā hu - the servant he)
divergences.textual_implication: Peshitta lacks the first-person possessive suffix found in MT, using instead emphatic state with independent pronoun. This creates distance between YHWH and the Servant figure, potentially reflecting discomfort with the intimate 'my servant' or representing a different Hebrew Vorlage reading עֶבֶד without suffix.

pesh_witness.overall_note: The Peshitta's treatment of Isaiah 53:11 shows complex relationships to both MT and LXX traditions. While lacking the explicit 'light' of 1QIsa-a and LXX, its structural features (coordination, plural 'righteous ones') suggest independent interpretive choices or a distinct Hebrew Vorlage. The transformation of 'my servant' to 'the servant' and pluralization of 'righteous' indicate theological sensitivity to the passage's messianic implications, characteristic of early Syriac translation technique that balances literalism with interpretive clarification for Christian communities.

synthesis: The textual witnesses to Isaiah 53:11 reveal significant pluriformity in the Second Temple period, with the most substantial variant being the presence or absence of אור ('light') after יראה. 1QIsa-a's inclusion of this word, supported by LXX's φῶς, demonstrates that at least two Hebrew text-forms circulated: one (proto-LXX/1QIsa-a) with 'he will see light and be satisfied,' and another (proto-MT) with 'he will see, he will be satisfied' where the object is implicit or omitted. The Peshitta occupies a middle position, lacking explicit 'light' but showing awareness of textual complexity through its morphological adjustments (plural 'righteous ones,' lack of possessive on 'servant'). The collective witness suggests the MT represents a secondary shortening, while the LXX-type text preserves an earlier, more complete reading that explicates the Servant's vindication through light imagery consistent with Isaiah's broader theology (Isaiah 9:2, 42:6, 49:6, 60:1-3).
synthesis_plain: The Dead Sea Scrolls show that ancient Hebrew copies of Isaiah 53:11 actually included the word 'light' ('he will see light'), which the Greek translation preserved but which was later dropped from the Hebrew text that became our standard Bible. The Syriac translation shows other differences, like making 'righteous one' plural, suggesting translators were trying to clarify a difficult passage about the suffering servant.
textual_history_implication: The evidence strongly suggests that the MT's shorter reading represents secondary development through either accidental omission (haplography of אור between יראה and ישבע) or deliberate theological reduction. The proto-LXX tradition, witnessed by 1QIsa-a, preserves the earlier, fuller text where 'light' serves as the grammatical object of 'see' and theologically explicates the Servant's post-suffering vindication. This case exemplifies how the Qumran biblical manuscripts demonstrate that the LXX occasionally translates a Hebrew text superior to MT, contradicting older assumptions that LXX variants always reflect translator freedom rather than Vorlage differences.

bibcrit_assessment.title: 1QIsa-a Confirms LXX Preserves Original 'Light' Reading
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The convergence of 1QIsa-a and LXX against MT in preserving אור/φῶς constitutes the most significant text-critical finding for Isaiah 53:11, fundamentally altering our understanding of the verse's original form and meaning. This is not a minor orthographic or morphological variant but a substantive lexical difference that affects both syntax (providing a direct object for 'see') and theology (explicating the nature of the Servant's vindication). The MT's omission creates a lectio difficilior only in the superficial sense; contextually and theologically, the reading with 'light' is lectio difficilior potior because it better explains the divergent tradition (MT could lose 'light' through haplography or deliberate shortening, but LXX+1QIsa-a are unlikely to independently add the same Hebrew word). Modern translations that follow MT here obscure the authentic prophetic vision of the Servant 'seeing light' after darkness.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The Dead Sea Scrolls prove that the original Hebrew of Isaiah 53:11 said the suffering servant would 'see light,' not just 'see' something unnamed. This changes how we understand the passage and shows that sometimes the ancient Greek translation preserved the correct reading when the traditional Hebrew text had lost a word.
